source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: When repair cost is counted, self-repair often does no better than plain resampling, especially at small budgets.
numbers: GPT-4 on APPS: 10 initial samples + 1 repair each (up to 20 total) = 1.05x pass@20 baseline; 2 initial + 10 repairs each (up to 22) = 0.97x pass@22. Models: CodeLlama-13b, GPT-3.5, GPT-4; HumanEval and APPS.
quote: Self-repair is not a silver bullet
limits: Repair rate and generation rate trend together; gain depends on task. Pass rates are bootstrapped.
agent_relevance: Spend budget on diverse fresh attempts, not long repair chains from one attempt. Supports keeping best-so-far and capping repair rounds.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) feedback quality experiment
finding: The bottleneck is the model's own diagnosis of the bug. A stronger feedback model unlocks repair gains.
numbers: Weaker coder + stronger feedback model (CodeLlama with GPT-3.5 or GPT-4 feedback; GPT-3.5 with GPT-4 feedback) beat both the i.i.d. baseline and self-repair at all budgets on APPS.
limits: Feedback model and coder are separated; costs counted in tokens.
agent_relevance: Mirrors the expert-novice gap: diagnosis (hypothesis formation) is what matters. Use a separate, stronger or independent diagnoser, and keep the fix step apart.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) human vs GPT-4 feedback study
finding: Expert human explanations of why code fails lead to far better repair than GPT-4's own explanations.
numbers: 16 participants, 2 feedbacks each for 40 failing GPT-4 programs, 25 repairs per feedback. Repair success overall 52.60% human vs 33.30% GPT-4 (1.58x). Introductory 62.21 vs 42.64; Interview 45.67 vs 19.33; Competition 14.67 vs 3.67. Only 2/80 human feedbacks held code or pseudocode.
limits: Volunteers, not matched to Gugerty-Olson expert level; gap grows with difficulty.
agent_relevance: Closest machine analogue of expert vs novice hypothesis quality. Good diagnosis is short natural language, not code.

source: Chen, Lin, Schaerli, Zhou (2023) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
finding: Letting the model explain its code line by line (rubber duck) and use test output improves accuracy; successes mostly end within 3 turns.
numbers: Spider text-to-SQL: +2-3% with explanation, +9% on hardest queries. TransCoder and MBPP with unit tests: up to +12%. Max 10 debug turns, successful runs mostly within 3. MBPP Codex baseline 72.2 (n=10) -> 75.6 with UT+Expl.
limits: Codex mainly; unit tests are the strong signal.
agent_relevance: Cap debug rounds (about 3). Explaining code before editing is an expert-like step that helped.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Self-Debug without execution
finding: Without unit-test execution the gains shrink for stronger models, and simple feedback can hurt.
numbers: Table 3 MBPP: Codex baseline 61.4 -> Simple 57.6 (down) -> +Expl 64.4 -> +Trace 66.2. GPT-3.5 67.6 -> 69.2. GPT-4 72.8 -> 76.4. TransCoder GPT-4 77.3 -> 78.4. Authors: GPT-4 gain about 3.6% on MBPP, about 1% elsewhere.
limits: Authors say models tend to be overconfident without execution.
agent_relevance: A revision not grounded in real output can add bugs, like novices (Codex 61.4 -> 57.6).

source: Chen et al. (2023) Self-Debug what gets fixed
finding: On TransCoder and MBPP, 60-70% of successful fixes repair an output mismatch where the initial code was already close.
numbers: Table 4b breakdown; max 10 turns, most successes within 3.
limits: Gains come mainly from near-correct code.
agent_relevance: Edit only a small distance from best-so-far; large rewrites rarely rescue.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Intrinsic self-correction (no outside signal) mostly hurts; reported gains came from oracle labels or weak first prompts.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 after round 1; GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7 over rounds. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0; HotpotQA 49 -> 49 -> 43.
limits: Reasoning tasks, not code; table values read from text extraction.
agent_relevance: Supports G2/G3: no revision from the model's opinion alone; extra rounds degrade, like novices adding bugs.

source: Huang et al. (2024) prompt-quality confound
finding: Some claimed self-correction gains came from a weak initial prompt, not from correction.
numbers: Paper states the improvement stems from sub-optimal prompts for the initial response; with a well-formed initial prompt self-correction lowers performance.
limits: GSM8K, CommonSenseQA, HotpotQA only.
agent_relevance: Always compare repair against a strong single-pass or best-of-N baseline.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Models are poor at finding the mistake but good at fixing it once the location is given. Random location does not help.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: 2186 CoT traces. Backtracking with oracle location raised accuracy on incorrect traces (e.g. +18.04 points in one table row); random locations hurt correct traces. Example: 50% baseline -> 68.6%; 99% baseline -> 92.8%.
limits: Oracle location needs a trained classifier in practice; gains depend on baseline accuracy.
agent_relevance: Localisation is the hard part; fixing is easy. Code, not the model, should locate the failing step (G2).

source: Tyen et al. (2024) bottleneck conclusion
finding: Authors conclude the main bottleneck of self-correction is identifying mistakes, not correcting them.
numbers: Oracle location helps; random location does not.
quote: the main bottleneck in self-correction methods is the identification of mistakes
limits: Needs a classifier for location in practice.
agent_relevance: Make the failing assertion or line an explicit input to the repair slot.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes?
finding: Critical survey: prompted self-feedback has not been shown to correct general tasks; success needs reliable external feedback or fine-tuning.
numbers: Survey of in-context and external-information self-correction; provides a checklist for fair evaluation (oracle stop signals, prompt strength).
limits: Survey; I read the abstract, intro and tables, not every section.
agent_relevance: Treat reported self-repair gains as unproven unless they use real execution or test signal.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine
finding: Generate, self-feedback, refine loop improves many tasks, but gains vary widely, and are tiny for strong models on code.
numbers: Average +20% absolute over one-step generation. Code Optimization: GPT-4 92.9 -> 93.1 (+0.2); ChatGPT 14.8 -> 23.0 (+8.2). Code Readability 37.4 -> 51.3. Generic feedback gave 26.0 vs 27.5 for specific feedback.
limits: Later critiques (Huang 2024) attribute some gains to prompt effects.
agent_relevance: Specific actionable feedback beats generic. Little room for gain when the base model is strong.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Verbal reflection on failed trials, kept in memory, improves agents when real environment or test feedback exists.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%; +22% AlfWorld, +20% HotPotQA, +11% HumanEval over baselines.
limits: Uses ground-truth or test signals to halt the loop (noted by Huang 2024 and Tyen 2024); read abstract, intro and result table only.
agent_relevance: Memory of failed hypotheses stops repeating a wrong one, like an expert.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: edit linter guard
finding: A linter that rejects an edit if it breaks syntax raises resolve rate: it blocks novice-style bug introduction.
numbers: Edit with linting 18.0% vs 15.0% without on SWE-bench Lite (+3.0). 12.47% (286/2294) full test set; 18.00% (54/300) Lite with GPT-4 Turbo. 1185/2294 (51.7%) trajectories have at least one failed edit.
quote: Linting is beneficial for stymieing cascading errors
limits: Single backbone; ablations on Lite 300 tasks.
agent_relevance: Reject edits that fail a code check before they land.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: early stopping and context ablations
finding: 93.0% of resolved instances are submitted before the cost limit; less history and summarised search do as well or better.
numbers: Lite: Summarized search 18.0 vs Iterative 12.0 vs No search 15.7; Last 5 observations 18.0 vs Full history 15.0; without demonstration 16.3.
limits: 1-3 point differences on 300 tasks may be noise.
agent_relevance: Most wins occur early, so cap rounds. Reading less, targeted, matches the expert pattern.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless
finding: A fixed pipeline of localise, repair, validate beat open-ended agents on cost and score; the model does not choose the next action.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite 32.00% (96/300) at $0.70 per issue.
limits: Lite has leaky or underspecified issues; authors build Lite-S.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis formation as a coded localisation stage before any edit.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless patch selection ablation
finding: Choosing the best among many candidate patches by tests gives most of the gain.
numbers: Majority vote 77 (25.67%); + regression tests 81 (27.00%); + reproduction tests 96 (32.00%). Cost $0.00, $0.01, $0.25 per issue.
limits: One benchmark, one backbone.
agent_relevance: Code selects best candidate with tests (G5); never trust the last edit by default.

source: Adnan and Kuhn (2025) The Debugging Decay Index
finding: Iterative LLM debugging decays exponentially; most models lose 60-80% of debugging effectiveness within 2-3 attempts.
numbers: 18 models on HumanEval, 6 attempts. Prior work cited: after the first attempt, 15 more yielded only 2.4% extra.
limits: HumanEval only (easy); preprint.
agent_relevance: Evidence for capping repair rounds at about 2-3 per candidate.

source: Adnan and Kuhn (2025) fresh start intervention
finding: Clearing the conversation and restarting with only the problem statement at the decay point raises final accuracy at equal attempts.
numbers: Six models: llama3.1:8b 72.56 -> 82.82; deepseek-coder-v2:16b 84.1 -> 92.1; Mistral:Instruct 54.3 -> 62.8 and 57.3 at two thresholds.
limits: Six models, HumanEval variants, preprint; gain size depends on timing.
agent_relevance: Restart from the problem, not from the broken draft, after 2-3 failed repairs; keep best-so-far.

source: Adnan and Kuhn (2025) reasoning models decay differently
finding: A reasoning-tuned model started lower in initial effectiveness than its base version.
numbers: phi4:14b E0=83.537 vs phi4-reasoning:14b E0=59.146; phi4 improved 21.95% vs 9.75% with iteration (as printed).
limits: Few models; decay-constant reading ambiguous in text extraction.
agent_relevance: Do not assume reasoning models repair better by iteration; measure per model.

source: Hellas et al. (2023) Responses of LLMs to Beginner Programmers' Help Requests
finding: LLMs find at least one real issue in most novice programs, but miss others and invent issues.
numbers: GPT-3.5: at least one real issue 90%; all issues 57%; non-existent issues 40%. Codex (English): 70% / 13% / 40%. Logic errors present in 108 help requests (72%).
limits: Student code from one Finnish course; Codex weak on Finnish prompts.
agent_relevance: 40% false-positive diagnoses mean the agent edits non-bugs; require the failing output to cite the location (G2).

source: Hellas et al. (2023) issue types and full solutions
finding: Models do better on logic issues than output formatting, and often hand over full solutions.
numbers: Per-theme hit rates between 35% and 73% in the paper (iteration 73%, arithmetic 57%, formatting 44%).
limits: Theme proportions partly ambiguous in text extraction.
agent_relevance: Ask for diagnosis only, not a rewritten solution.

source: Tian et al. (2024) DebugBench overall and by bug count
finding: Zero-shot LLM debugging is below human; more simultaneous bugs means lower pass rate.
numbers: GPT-4-0613 passes 75.0%, GPT-3.5 62.1%. GPT-4 by type: missing colons 93.6, condition error 73.1, double bugs 70.7, triple 58.9, quadruple 55.9. Human 12 raters solved 8/12 to 12/12 per type. Model under 10 s per bug vs about 20 min for humans.
limits: Bugs implanted by GPT-4 on LeetCode, not real; 12 human raters.
agent_relevance: Fix one bug per round: fits limit-edits-per-round.

source: Tian et al. (2024) DebugBench runtime feedback
finding: Runtime feedback helps syntax and reference bugs but not logic bugs.
numbers: Finding 3 in conclusion; effect shown in Figure 4 on gpt-4-0613 (values not extracted).
quote: Runtime feedback enhanced the debugging performance for syntax and reference errors but is unhelpful for logical errors
limits: Figure values not read.
agent_relevance: Logic faults need hypothesis tests, not only error text.

source: Tian et al. (2024) DebugBench coding vs debugging
finding: Coding and debugging ability are correlated; for logic or multiple bugs debugging can be as hard as generation.
numbers: Phi-coefficient analysis reported; values not extracted.
limits: Values not read.
agent_relevance: A model that cannot write the solution will rarely debug it; repair does not close capability gaps.

source: Gugerty and Olson (1986) Debugging by skilled and novice programmers
finding: Human anchor only: experts debug faster and form better hypotheses; novices more often add new bugs. Not opened by this angle.
numbers: No numbers recorded here; see the human-angle evidence files.
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: The machine results above are the AI analogue of novice-like repeated blind edits.
